o: We have an n×n deck (n² cells) and containers of weight w each. We may load as many containers as fit both by cells and by weight, so the answer is simply the smaller of the cell limit n² and the weight limit ⌊maxWeight / w⌋. Example 1: n²=4, ⌊15/3⌋=5, so min is 4. Example 2: n²=9, ⌊20/5⌋=4, so min is 4. Constraints are tiny (n ≤ 1000, values fit easily in 64-bit), so even a simulation loop works; the formula is O(1).
k: Each container is identical, so only counts matter — no arrangement issues.
The binding constraint is min(cell capacity, weight capacity).

a.i: Since every container weighs exactly w, at most maxWeight // w fit by weight and at most n*n fit by cells. The answer is the minimum of these two bounds.
Load containers one at a time while cells and weight budget remain; this mirrors the physical process and yields the same count.
s: While cnt < n*n and (cnt+1)*w <= maxWeight, increment cnt.
a.t: O(min(n², maxWeight/w)) — one iteration per loaded container.

w: Use the formula in an interview; mention simulation only as a sanity check. Pitfall: overflow when computing n*n or maxWeight/w in fixed-width languages (use 64-bit intermediates). Follow-ups: what if containers had different weights (then it becomes a greedy/sort by weight), or if cells had individual weight limits.
